pdm-ischemia-infarction: What is often the very first sign of cardiac ischemia on the tracing?
Hyperacute T waves
How are hyperacute T waves described?
Broad, tall and symmetrical
How does a normal T wave differ from a hyperacute one?
It is asymmetrical, with a slow upstroke and sharper fall
What does ST-segment depression represent?
Subendocardial ischemia
What does ST-segment elevation represent?
Transmural ischemia, also called injury
What do pathologic Q waves usually represent?
Infarction: death of cardiac tissue
Can pathologic Q waves reflect an old event?
Yes; they come from a previous or an acute event
Which duration makes a Q wave pathologic?
Longer than 0.04 seconds, one small box
Which depth makes a Q wave pathologic?
Deeper than 2 mm, or more than 25% of the R wave
What is a single negative deflection with no R wave called?
A QS complex, a pathologic Q wave usually meaning infarction
Where is the J point?
Where the QRS meets the ST segment
Where do the J point and ST segment sit in a healthy heart?
At the baseline
What is the J point compared with to judge ST deviation?
The TP segment
At a fast rate with no TP segment, what is the J point compared with?
The onset of the QRS complex
Into which two branches does the left coronary artery divide?
The circumflex and the left anterior descending
Which artery supplies the right ventricle and the bottom of the left ventricle?
The right coronary artery
Which artery supplies the side and back of the left ventricle?
The circumflex artery
Which artery supplies the front of the left ventricle and septum?
The left anterior descending artery
Which leads view the inferior wall?
II, III and aVF
Which leads view the septal wall?
V1 and V2
Which leads view the anterior wall?
V3 and V4
Which leads view the lateral wall?
I, aVL, V5 and V6
Which leads view the high lateral wall?
I and aVL
What are the reciprocal leads of an inferior infarction?
I and aVL
What are the reciprocal leads of a lateral infarction?
II, III and aVF
Which territories have no direct reciprocal leads?
Septal, anterior and anteroseptal
Which leads carry the reciprocal changes of a posterior infarction?
V1, V2, V3 and V4
Which lead is not assigned to any wall?
aVR
What defines an ST-elevation myocardial infarction?
1 mm or more in two or more contiguous leads
What are reciprocal changes?
The mirror image of the event on the opposite leads
How is ST depression read when ST elevation is also present?
As a reciprocal change until proven otherwise
Does an absence of reciprocal changes exclude ischemia?
No; they confirm but are not required
What should isolated ST depression in V1 to V4 be considered?
A posterior infarction until proven otherwise
How is a posterior tracing obtained?
Move V4, V5 and V6 to the back as V7, V8 and V9
What confirms a posterior wall infarction?
ST elevation in V7 to V9
Which artery is typically occluded in a posterior infarction?
The left circumflex artery
What share of infarctions are isolated posterior ones?
Which findings suggest right ventricular involvement?
Hypotension, clear lungs and jugular vein distension
Where is V4R placed?
Right fifth intercostal space, midclavicular line
What confirms right ventricular involvement?
ST elevation in V4R
Which artery's inferior infarction can include the right ventricle?
The right coronary artery
What is a posterior tracing with V7 to V9 sometimes called?
A 15-lead electrocardiogram
